# About ContentFellow
ContentFellow is a UK marketing service for small businesses, based in Burnley, Lancashire. Instead of agency retainers, you hire "Fellows": specialists on simple monthly plans from £59, for photo and video, editing, social media, websites, and SEO & GEO (getting recommended by Google and AI assistants like ChatGPT).

## Key facts
Name | ContentFellow (one word; not related to Contentful, the software company) | 
What it is | A UK marketing service for small businesses, sold as monthly plans called "Fellows" | 
Based in | Burnley, Lancashire, United Kingdom | 
Serves | Small businesses and creators across the UK; on-site shoots within about 20 miles of Burnley | 
Founded | 2026 | 
Prices | From £59 a month; full team £389 a month | 
Billing | Monthly; add, remove or upgrade Fellows from the next month | 
Free trial | Every Fellow has a free trial; no card needed | 
VAT | Not VAT registered: prices shown are the full amount, no VAT added | 
Website | https://contentfellow.com/ |

# Affordable SEO and GEO Services for UK Small Businesses: 2026 Price Comparison

Quick answer: Affordable SEO for a UK small business usually costs £89 to £400 a month. Budget packages start around £89–£150, local SEO plans from specialist agencies typically cost £250–£400, and managed agency campaigns start around £1,000. In 2026, a good affordable plan should also cover GEO (getting named by ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity), not just Google. (Updated October 2026. Prices are as published by each provider on 16 October 2026; check their sites for current offers.)

Transparency note: this comparison is written by ContentFellow, and our Search Fellow plan is included. We've only listed prices that providers publish themselves, and we explain how to judge every option, including ours.

## UK affordable SEO prices compared (published prices)

Provider / type | 
Published starting price | 
Notes | 

ContentFellow Search Fellow | 
£89 a month | 
SEO + GEO in one plan, monthly billing, free 7-day trial | 

Wrise | 
"Low cost £99 packages" | 
Budget SEO packages for small businesses | 

Polaris (guide) | 
From about £300 a month | 
For smaller local campaigns, per their UK pricing guide | 

ZainSEO | 
From about £295 a month | 
London-focused, local and technical SEO | 

Dandy Marketing | 
£399 a month (Local) | 
Fixed local package for one town or area | 

ClickIntelligence | 
From £1,000 a month | 
Managed SEO campaigns | 

Typical UK SEO/GEO agency | 
£1,100–£3,800 a month | 
See our LLM optimisation cost guide | 

What the table can't show is scope. Two £300 plans can include very different amounts of work, so use the checklist below before comparing prices.

## What should affordable SEO include in 2026?

### 1. Clear monthly deliverables

"Ongoing optimisation" isn't a deliverable. Ask for numbers: how many pages written or improved, which technical fixes, how many directory listings cleaned up, each month.

### 2. AI search (GEO), not just Google

ChatGPT's live search leans on Bing's index, and its answers mostly cite websites, directories and "best of" lists. An affordable plan in 2026 should include Bing Webmaster Tools, structured data (schema), answer-first service pages and checking whether AI assistants mention you. Our guide on how to get recommended by ChatGPT explains why.

### 3. Monthly reporting you can understand

You should see rankings, clicks from Google Search Console, and which AI prompts name you versus competitors. If a report is only "traffic is up", ask for more.

### 4. Fair terms

Check the minimum term (monthly vs 6–12 months), who owns the content and accounts if you leave, and whether there's a trial or a way to see the work before committing.

## Red flags in cheap SEO

- Guaranteed #1 rankings. Nobody controls Google or ChatGPT. Guarantees usually mean tiny keywords nobody searches.

- "1,000 backlinks for £50". Bulk links from spam sites can get you penalised.

- No access to your own accounts. You should own your Google Business Profile, Search Console and website.

- Long contracts with no deliverables. Twelve months of "optimisation" with no written scope is hard to hold anyone to.

- No mention of AI search. In 2026, a plan that ignores ChatGPT and Google's AI Overviews is only doing half the job.

## Which level is right for you?

Your situation | 
Sensible budget | 

Sole trader or new local business | 
DIY (free) or £89–£150 a month | 

Established local business in one town | 
£89–£400 a month | 

Several locations or competitive industry (law, dental, trades in big cities) | 
£400–£1,000 a month | 

National or ecommerce business | 
£1,000+ a month | 

Not sure if you need GEO, SEO or both? Read GEO vs SEO: what's the difference.

## How the Search Fellow compares

Billing is monthly, you approve changes before they go live, and you can try it free for 7 days (AI visibility check, Bing set-up, AI crawler access and a Google Business Profile tidy; you keep every fix). It suits small businesses; if you need large-scale digital PR or hundreds of pages, a bigger agency budget makes more sense.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does affordable SEO cost in the UK?

Most UK small businesses pay £89 to £400 a month for affordable SEO. Managed agency campaigns usually start around £1,000 a month.

### Are £99 SEO packages worth it?

They can be, if the deliverables are clear and the work is real: technical fixes, service pages, listings and reporting. Avoid any package that relies on bulk backlinks or guarantees rankings.

### What is the cheapest way to do SEO for a small business?

Do the basics yourself: claim your Google Business Profile and Bing Places, add your services with prices and locations to your website, collect reviews, and verify Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. It's free, but takes time.

### Does affordable SEO include ChatGPT and AI search?

Not always. Ask whether the plan includes Bing indexing, structured data and AI visibility tracking. The ContentFellow Search Fellow includes all three.

### How long does affordable SEO take to work?

Technical fixes show within weeks; rankings and AI mentions usually take 3 to 6 months to build, depending on competition in your area.

### Can I cancel an SEO contract?

It depends on the provider; many ask for 6 to 12 months. ContentFellow bills monthly and you can cancel from the next month.

# How Much Does App Development Cost in the UK? (2026 Prices)

Quick answer: In the UK, a simple app built by an agency usually costs £8,000 to £40,000, a medium-complexity app £40,000 to £80,000, and a complex app £80,000 or more. Keeping it running costs roughly £149 to £1,495 a month. Small businesses can start far cheaper with a web app (from about £1,249) or a fixed-price iPhone and Android app (from £3,499 with ContentFellow). (Prices as of October 2026.)

## How much does it cost to build an app in the UK?

Type of app | 
Typical UK agency price | 
Timeline | 
Good for | 

Design and clickable prototype only | 
£3,000–£12,000 | 
2–4 weeks | 
Testing an idea with investors or customers | 

Simple app or MVP | 
£8,000–£40,000 | 
4–8 weeks | 
Bookings, loyalty, a single clear job | 

Medium-complexity app | 
£40,000–£80,000 | 
2–4 months | 
Accounts, payments, admin panel, integrations | 

Complex or enterprise app | 
£80,000–£200,000+ | 
4+ months | 
Marketplaces, real-time features, heavy compliance | 

Where the numbers come from. UK studios publish wide but consistent ranges: Fulminous puts a simple MVP at £8,000–£15,000, Foresight Mobile quotes £15,000–£40,000 for a simple app and £40,000–£80,000 for medium complexity, and Appinventiv's UK range runs from £23,780 to over £198,000. Pixelfield puts design and prototyping alone at £3,000–£12,000.

## What does it cost to keep an app running?

Most owners forget this part. Once an app is live it needs hosting, fixes when Apple and Google update their systems, and small improvements.

- Store fees: the Apple Developer Program is £79 a year in the UK; Google Play charges a one-off $25.

- Hosting and backend: usually £10–£100 a month for a small app.

- Maintenance plans: specialist UK studios such as Foresight Mobile charge £675–£1,495 a month. Smaller providers charge less: ContentFellow's app management plans run from £149 to £599 a month.

## What makes an app more expensive?

- Platforms. A web app works on every phone from the browser. Native iPhone and Android apps cost more. Building both from one codebase (cross-platform) typically saves 30–40% compared with two separate apps.

- Screens and features. Every login, payment, booking calendar, chat or map adds days of design, build and testing.

- Backend. A database, admin panel, integrations with your other tools and push notifications are often half the work.

- Upkeep. Plan for monthly care from day one so the app doesn't break after the next iOS update.

## Is there a cheaper way for a small business to get an app?

Yes. Many small businesses don't need a £40,000 app. Three cheaper routes:

- A web app (PWA). Customers add it to their home screen like an app, with no app store needed. Ideal for bookings, loyalty cards and client portals.

- A fixed-price simple app. Agree a tight list of screens up front instead of paying by the hour.

- Start small, then grow. Launch the version that does one job well, then add features on a monthly plan.

# How to Check if ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity Mention Your Business (UK Guide)

Quick answer: Write down 10 to 20 questions your customers ask, put each one into ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Copilot in a fresh, logged-out chat, and record whether your business is named, in what position, and which competitors and websites are cited instead. It takes about 20 minutes. Repeat it monthly, or use a tracking tool to do it at scale. (Updated October 2026.)

## Why check at all?

More customers now ask an AI assistant "who's the best…" or "how much does… cost in the UK" before they search Google. The assistant usually names only two or three businesses. If you're not one of them, you won't see it in Google Analytics: the customer simply never arrives.

## The 20-minute AI visibility test

### 1. List the questions your customers ask

Mix three types:
- Price questions: "How much does a wedding videographer cost in Lancashire?"
- Best-of questions: "Best social media manager for small businesses in the UK"
- Problem questions: "How do I get more bookings for my salon?"

Use your customers' words, not your industry jargon. Aim for 10 to 20 prompts.

### 2. Ask each AI assistant

Use ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Microsoft Copilot. Open a fresh chat, log out or use a private window so past chats don't skew results, and keep your location set to the UK.

### 3. Record the results

For every prompt, note in a simple spreadsheet:
- Were you named? (yes/no)
- In what position? (1st, 2nd, 3rd…)
- Which competitors were named?
- Which websites were cited as sources? (These are your targets.)

Your share of voice is the percentage of answers that name you. Most small businesses start at zero, and that's normal.

### 4. Fix the gaps and repeat monthly

Look at the cited sources. If AI keeps quoting the same directory, review site or "best UK…" article, getting listed there is your fastest win. Then re-run the same prompts next month and compare.

## Can you see AI traffic in Google Analytics?

Partly. In GA4, open Reports → Acquisition → Traffic acquisition and look for referrals from chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, gemini.google.com and copilot.microsoft.com. Many AI answers don't send a click at all, so treat this as a floor, not the full picture.

## Tools that track AI visibility at scale

Running 20 prompts across four assistants every week by hand gets tedious. Tools such as OpenSEO, Semrush and Similarweb track prompts automatically and chart your share of voice against competitors. Costs vary with how many prompts and engines you track: as a guide, checking 12 prompts across 5 AI engines costs us roughly $3.50 per run.

## What to do if AI doesn't mention you

- Make sure your site lets AI crawlers in and loads fast.

- Add structured data with your services and prices in pounds.

- Publish one clear, answer-first page for each key customer question.

- Earn mentions on the sites AI already cites: reviews, UK directories, best-of lists and local press.

More detail: how to get your business recommended by ChatGPT and llms.txt explained.

Ask ChatGPT the questions your customers ask, in a fresh logged-out chat, and see whether your business is named. Repeat across several questions and record the results.

### Why does ChatGPT recommend my competitors and not me?

Usually because competitors are mentioned on more trusted sites (reviews, directories, best-of lists) and have clearer pages answering the exact question.

# GEO vs SEO: What's the Difference, and Do UK Small Businesses Need Both? (2026)

Quick answer: SEO (search engine optimisation) gets your website ranked on Google so people click through to you. GEO (generative engine optimisation) gets your business named inside AI answers from ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews. Most of the work overlaps, so UK small businesses should do both together rather than pay for them separately. (Updated October 2026.)

## First, which "GEO" are we talking about?

Search for "GEO vs SEO" and some pages explain geographic targeting, meaning ranking in a particular town or country. That's usually called local SEO.

In 2026, GEO almost always means generative engine optimisation: making your business easy for AI assistants to find, trust and recommend. It's also called AEO (answer engine optimisation), LLMO or AI SEO. This guide uses that meaning.

## What's the difference between GEO and SEO?

The simplest way to put it: SEO wins a click, GEO wins a mention. On Google, people see a list of links and choose one. In an AI answer, the assistant reads many sources and names two or three businesses. Often nobody clicks anything; the recommendation is the result.

 | 
SEO | 
GEO | 

Where you show up | 
Google and Bing results pages | 
ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews | 

What you win | 
A ranking and a click to your site | 
A mention or citation inside the answer | 

What the engine looks for | 
Relevant pages, links, speed, good user signals | 
Clear facts, structured data, consistent mentions on trusted sites | 

How you measure it | 
Rankings, clicks and impressions in Search Console | 
Share of AI answers that name you for your key prompts | 

How fast it moves | 
Usually 3 to 6 months | 
Days for AI tools that search live; months to become a regular recommendation | 

Typical UK small-business cost | 
Often bundled; standalone SEO retainers vary widely | 
£89 to £400 a month on a combined plan (see full price guide) | 

## How much of the work overlaps?

A lot. We estimate around 70% of the effort is shared, because both kinds of engine need the same foundations:

- Crawler access. Google needs to crawl your site; so do GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot. One robots.txt and one sitemap serve both.

- Structured data. Organisation, Service, FAQ and Article schema help Google show rich results and help AI tools quote your facts correctly, including your prices in pounds.

- Answer-first pages. A page that answers the question in its first sentence ranks better on Google and gets quoted more by AI.

- Trusted mentions. Reviews, directory listings and articles on other UK sites build authority for Google and give AI assistants confidence to name you.

The part that's genuinely different is measurement and a few GEO-only tasks: tracking which AI prompts mention you, adding an llms.txt file, and getting listed on the "best of" pages that AI assistants like to cite.

## Do UK small businesses need both?

For most, yes, and doing them together is cheaper than doing them apart. Here's how to decide what to lean on first:

- Local trades and services (plumbers, salons, clinics): start with SEO and Google Business Profile, then add GEO. Many local searches still end on Google Maps.

- Professional and online services (agencies, consultants, coaches, SaaS): lean on GEO early. Buyers increasingly ask ChatGPT "who's the best…" before they search.

- Brand-new websites: do the shared foundations first. Neither SEO nor GEO works until search engines and AI crawlers can read your site.

- Businesses already ranking on Google: add GEO now. You've built most of the foundation, and AI answers are where your competitors aren't measuring yet.

## How should you split a small budget?

If you pay for help, buy one plan that covers both rather than two suppliers. A sensible split for a UK small business:

- About 70% on shared foundations: technical fixes, structured data, answer-first content.

- About 20% on mentions: reviews, UK directories and pitching "best of" lists.

- About 10% on AI visibility tracking: checking each month which prompts name you and which name competitors.

Similarweb suggests small businesses put 10 to 20% of their search budget into AI visibility. Our split sits inside that range, because most GEO work is also SEO work.

For pound-by-pound prices, see our guide: how much LLM optimisation costs UK small businesses.

## Is SEO dead because of AI search?

No. Google still sends most website traffic for most UK businesses, and AI assistants often build their answers from pages that already rank well. What's changed is that ranking alone isn't enough: you also want to be the business the AI names. That's why the two belong together.

SEO helps your website rank in Google and Bing results so people click through. GEO helps your business get named inside AI-generated answers from ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity.

### Does GEO mean geographic SEO?

Not usually, in 2026. GEO now most often means generative engine optimisation for AI search. Optimising for a location is normally called local SEO.

# How to Get Your Business Recommended by ChatGPT: A UK Step-by-Step Guide (2026)

Quick answer: You can't pay ChatGPT to recommend your business, and there's no form to submit. ChatGPT names businesses it can find and trust: it reads your website, Bing's search results, directories, reviews and "best of" lists. To get recommended, make your site clear and crawlable, get indexed on Bing, keep your details identical across UK directories, collect reviews, and get mentioned on lists ChatGPT already cites. Then check the same prompts every month. (Updated October 2026.)

## Where does ChatGPT get its business recommendations?

ChatGPT answers from two places: what the model learned in training, and a live web search it runs for current or buying questions. That search uses OpenAI's own crawler (OAI-SearchBot) and search partners, mainly Bing's index, not Google's. If Bing can't find you, ChatGPT's live search usually can't either.

What it cites is mostly not your blog:

- A Yext study of 6.8 million AI citations (October 2025) found 44% came from businesses' own websites and 42% from listings and directories. Only 14% came from other third-party sites.

- In a 2026 study of 9,434 ChatGPT answers about local services in the US and Canada, Cheers found 84% of answers with citations cited a directory, review site or "best of" list. When ChatGPT cited a business's own site, it linked the homepage (37%) or a service page (24%), and a blog post only 1% of the time.

Those studies are North American, but the lesson carries over to the UK: your homepage, your service pages and your directory listings do the heavy lifting.

## Step 1: Check what ChatGPT says about you today

Open a new chat (logged out, or in a private window) and ask what your customers would ask. Write down who gets named, and which sources are linked.

- "Best [your service] in [your town]"

- "Who should I use for [the problem you solve] in [your area]?"

- "Affordable [your service] for small businesses in the UK"

- "Is [your business name] any good?"

- "[Your business name] vs [a competitor]"

Use 10 to 12 prompts and keep them in a spreadsheet. This is your baseline. The sites ChatGPT links are your to-do list.

## Step 2: Let the AI crawlers in

Check yourdomain.co.uk/robots.txt. It must not block OAI-SearchBot (ChatGPT search), GPTBot (OpenAI training), Bingbot, ClaudeBot or PerplexityBot. Some website builders and security plugins block them by default.

Then verify your site in Bing Webmaster Tools (free, it can import from Google Search Console in a few clicks), submit your sitemap, and switch on IndexNow so new pages reach Bing in hours rather than weeks.

## Step 3: Make your homepage and service pages answer-first

ChatGPT quotes pages that state facts plainly. On your homepage and each service page, say in the first two sentences:

- What you do, in the words customers use

- Where you work: town, county, or "UK-wide"

- Who it's for

- What it costs, in pounds, even as a "from" price

Give each main service its own page, and add a page per town if you serve several areas. A page called "Wedding videographer in Burnley" is easier to cite than a homepage that tries to say everything.

## Step 4: Add structured data

Structured data (schema markup) is code that tells machines your facts directly. Add Organization or LocalBusiness (name, address, phone, area served), Service with an Offer in GBP, and FAQPage for your common questions. Test it with Google's Rich Results Test; Bing reads the same markup.

## Step 5: Make your details identical across UK directories

AI engines cross-check. If your name, address and phone number differ between sites, they trust you less. Use exactly the same business name, address, phone and one-line description on:

Directory | 
Who it's for | 
Cost | 

Google Business Profile | 
Everyone | 
Free | 

Bing Places for Business | 
Everyone (feeds Bing) | 
Free | 

Apple Business Connect | 
Everyone (Apple Maps, Siri) | 
Free | 

Yell, Thomson Local, Scoot | 
Local services | 
Free basic listing | 

Trustpilot | 
Everyone | 
Free basic plan | 

Checkatrade, TrustATrader, MyBuilder | 
Trades | 
Paid membership | 

Clutch, DesignRush | 
Agencies and B2B | 
Free profile | 

Companies House, LinkedIn | 
Limited companies, B2B | 
Free | 

## Step 6: Collect reviews on more than one platform

ChatGPT reads what reviews say, not just the stars. A business with recent reviews on Google, Trustpilot and an industry site looks safer than one with reviews in a single place. Ask happy customers to mention the service and the town in their own words ("great kitchen fitter in Preston"), because that's how the AI matches you to a prompt.

## Step 7: Get onto the lists ChatGPT already cites

Go back to the sources from Step 1. If ChatGPT keeps citing "10 best [service] in Manchester" articles, contact those sites and ask to be considered. Also try:

- Your local newspaper or business magazine (a short story or expert quote)

- Trade associations and chambers of commerce (member directories)

- Supplier and partner pages ("our recommended installers")

- Honest, helpful answers on Reddit and forums where your customers ask questions

One mention on a list ChatGPT already trusts can do more than ten new blog posts.

## Step 8: Track the same prompts every month

Re-run your Step 1 prompts once a month and note who's named. In GA4, look for visits from chatgpt.com and perplexity.ai under traffic acquisition. And ask every new customer how they found you; "ChatGPT told me" is now a real answer.

## Do you still need Google SEO?

Yes. Most of these steps also lift your Google rankings, and Google still sends most website traffic. The two work best together, which we explain in GEO vs SEO: what's the difference for UK small businesses.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I pay to be recommended by ChatGPT?

No. There's no advertising product, listing fee or submission form that places a business in ChatGPT's recommendations. You get named by being easy to find and widely trusted online.

### Does ChatGPT use Google to find businesses?

Not mainly. ChatGPT's live search uses OpenAI's own crawler and Bing's index, so verify your site in Bing Webmaster Tools and claim Bing Places as well as Google Business Profile.

### How long does it take to get recommended by ChatGPT?

Technical fixes can reach Bing within days, but reviews and third-party mentions build up over weeks. Most small businesses should allow 6 to 12 weeks before judging results.

### Does this work for local businesses in the UK?

Yes. Local prompts like "best plumber in Leeds" lean heavily on directories, reviews and pages that name a service and a town, all things a small local business can control.

### How do I check if ChatGPT recommends my business?

Ask it the questions your customers would ask, in a fresh logged-out chat, and record who it names each month. Check GA4 for visits from chatgpt.com too.

### Do I need an agency to get recommended by ChatGPT?

No. Every step in this guide can be done yourself. A monthly plan saves time and adds tracking across several AI engines; it shouldn't cost thousands.

# How Much Does LLM Optimisation Cost for Small Businesses? (UK Prices, 2026)

Quick answer: In the UK, LLM optimisation (also called GEO or AI search optimisation) costs a small business roughly £0–£100 a month DIY, £89–£400 a month on a productised plan, £300–£1,000 a month with a freelancer, and £1,100–£3,800 a month with a traditional agency. Most small businesses get the best return from a £89–£400 monthly plan that combines SEO and GEO with a monthly AI visibility report. (Prices as of October 2026.)

## What is LLM optimisation (and what isn't it)?

LLM optimisation is the work of making your business easy for large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity to find, understand and recommend when someone asks them a question. You'll also see it called GEO (generative engine optimisation), AEO (answer engine optimisation), LLMO or AI SEO. They all describe the same goal: being the business the AI names in its answer.

Two things share the name and are not covered here:

- LLM cost optimisation for developers (cutting the API bill of an AI app).

- The LLM degree (Master of Laws).

If you're a small business owner wondering why ChatGPT recommends a competitor instead of you, you're in the right place.

## How much does LLM optimisation cost in the UK?

Almost every price guide on page one of Google quotes US agencies in dollars. Here is the same market translated into what a UK small business actually pays. US figures are converted at roughly $1 = £0.76 and rounded.

Option |

Where the numbers come from. WebFX, Nutshell and TeamAI all put small-business GEO retainers at $1,500–$5,000 a month (about £1,100–£3,800). A study of 60 agency price lists by Seotal found the median entry AI SEO package was $750 a month (about £570), with the middle half between $461 and $2,000, and software plans starting at $29 a month. Practitioners on Reddit report one-off GEO setups from $500 to $7,200.

## What drives the price up or down?

- How competitive your category is. A plumber in Leeds needs far less work than a London law firm or a SaaS brand.

- How many markets you target. UK-only is cheaper. Adding Ireland, Germany or France multiplies content and tracking.

- Content volume. AI engines cite pages that answer questions clearly. More questions to cover means more pages.

- Digital PR and mentions. LLMs trust brands that other trusted sites mention. Earning those mentions is the most expensive part of agency retainers.

- Reporting depth. Tracking dozens of prompts across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity every day costs more than a monthly spot check.

- The state of your website. Slow pages, missing structured data or blocked AI crawlers need fixing first, usually as a one-off.

## What should a small business budget for GEO?

A simple rule: spend 10–20% of your search budget on AI visibility, which Similarweb recommends for small and local businesses. If you have no search budget yet, start like this:

- Under £100 a month: do it yourself. Fix the basics below and track a handful of prompts.

- £89–£400 a month: hire a productised plan that does SEO and GEO together. This is where most UK small businesses see the best return, because the same work (clear pages, structured data, reviews, mentions) lifts both Google rankings and AI recommendations.

- £1,000+ a month: only once you've proven that search brings you customers and you need digital PR at scale.

Not sure whether you need GEO, SEO or both? Read GEO vs SEO: what's the difference for UK small businesses.

## What's included in a good LLM optimisation plan?

Whatever you pay, check the plan covers these four layers:

- Technical access. AI crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended) allowed in robots.txt, fast pages, an llms.txt file, clean sitemap.

- Structured data. Organisation, LocalBusiness, Product or Service, FAQ and Article schema so machines read your facts correctly.

- Answer-ready content. Pages that answer real customer questions in the first two sentences, with prices, comparisons and dates stated plainly.

- Authority and tracking. Reviews, directory listings and mentions on trusted UK sites, plus a monthly report showing which AI prompts mention you and which mention competitors.

If a quote doesn't say how it measures AI visibility, ask. "We'll improve your AI presence" isn't a deliverable.

## How to do LLM optimisation yourself (free to £100 a month)

If your budget is close to zero, these steps cover 80% of the basics:

- Search ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity for the five questions your customers ask most. Note who gets recommended.

- Make sure your robots.txt doesn't block AI crawlers.

- Add FAQ and LocalBusiness schema (free plugins exist for most site builders).

- Write one page per key question with the answer in the first sentence, and a price where you can.

- Get listed and reviewed on the UK directories and review sites your sector uses.

- Repeat step 1 every month and track the change.

## Is LLM optimisation worth it for a small business?

For most UK small businesses, yes, if the cost stays proportionate. More buyers now ask an AI assistant for a recommendation before they search Google, and the assistant usually names only two or three businesses. Being one of them is worth more than ranking eighth on Google. The risk is overpaying. A £3,000-a-month agency retainer rarely makes sense for a business turning over less than £500,000 a year. A £89–£400 plan that does SEO and GEO together usually does.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does GEO cost for a small business in the UK?

Most UK small businesses pay between £89 and £400 a month for a productised SEO and GEO plan. Traditional agency retainers cost about £1,100–£3,800 a month, and DIY with tools costs £0–£100 a month.

### Is LLM optimisation the same as SEO?

No, but they overlap. SEO aims to rank pages on Google, while LLM optimisation aims to get your brand named in AI answers. Both rely on clear content, structured data and trusted mentions, so doing them together is cheaper than paying for each separately.

### What is LLM search optimisation called?

It goes by several names: GEO (generative engine optimisation), AEO (answer engine optimisation), LLMO (large language model optimisation) and AI SEO. They describe the same practice.

### How long does LLM optimisation take to work?

Technical fixes and structured data can be picked up within weeks, as AI tools that search the web live (Perplexity, ChatGPT search, Gemini) read new pages quickly. Becoming a consistent recommendation usually takes three to six months of content and mentions.

### Can I do LLM optimisation myself?

Yes. Allowing AI crawlers, adding schema, writing answer-first pages and collecting reviews cost little beyond your time. Most owners hire help when they need regular content and monthly tracking across several AI platforms.

### Why do US price guides quote such high prices?

They quote US agency retainers for US businesses, usually $1,500–$5,000 a month. UK productised plans are cheaper because they offer fixed deliverables instead of open-ended agency hours.

### How do I know if ChatGPT recommends my business?

Ask it the questions your customers ask, in a fresh chat, and note who it names. A proper plan tracks dozens of these prompts across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity every month and reports your share of mentions against competitors.

# llms.txt Explained: Should Your Small Business Have One? (2026)

Quick answer: llms.txt is a plain text file at the root of a website that lists its most important pages for AI tools. It takes about 10 minutes to add and does no harm, but it does not improve Google rankings or AI Overviews, and there's no evidence it gets you mentioned more by ChatGPT or Gemini. Treat it as an optional extra, not a GEO strategy. (Updated October 2026.)

## What is llms.txt?

llms.txt is a proposed standard, introduced by Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI in September 2024. It's a short Markdown file at yoursite.com/llms.txt that gives AI systems a curated list of your key pages, each with a one-line description: a table of contents written for machines.

It isn't the same as robots.txt, which tells crawlers what they may or may not access. llms.txt can't block anything.

## Does llms.txt help SEO or AI visibility?

Not in any measurable way, based on what's public in 2026:

- Google: on 15 June 2026 Google added guidance to its AI optimisation documentation saying llms.txt has no effect on Search rankings or AI Overviews. Google's John Mueller has compared it to the old meta keywords tag.

- Research: an SE Ranking study of 300,000 domains found about 10% had an llms.txt file and that having one didn't predict AI citations.

- Bot logs: OtterlyAI recorded 84 visits to llms.txt out of 62,100 AI bot requests over 90 days. AI search crawlers mostly read your normal HTML pages.

- No major AI company (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta or Perplexity) had publicly confirmed that its answer engine reads the file as of early 2026.

Where it does get used is by AI coding assistants (such as Cursor and GitHub Copilot) reading developer documentation. That matters for software companies, not for most local businesses.

## Should a small business add one?

If your website provider can add it in a few minutes, fine: it's harmless, and it's a tidy summary of your services and prices. But if someone is charging you extra for "llms.txt optimisation" as a way to rank in ChatGPT, be sceptical.

## What actually gets you mentioned by ChatGPT and Gemini?

- Let AI crawlers in. Make sure robots.txt allows GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot, and that your pages load fast.

- Structured data. Organisation, Service and FAQ schema with your real prices in pounds.

- Answer-first pages. Answer the customer's question in the first sentence, one page per question.

- Trusted mentions. Reviews, UK directories, "best of" lists and local press. AI assistants lean heavily on these.

For a step-by-step version, read how to get your business recommended by ChatGPT and GEO vs SEO.

## How to add an llms.txt file (if you want one)

Create a text file called llms.txt with your business name, one line on what you do, then a list of your key pages with a short description, and upload it to your site's root folder. Keep it accurate and update it when prices change.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is llms.txt?

A Markdown file at the root of a website that lists its key pages with short descriptions so AI tools can find them. It was proposed by Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI in 2024.

### Does llms.txt improve Google rankings?

No. Google said in June 2026 that llms.txt has no effect on Search rankings or AI Overviews.

### Does ChatGPT read llms.txt?

There's no public confirmation that ChatGPT's answer engine uses it. Studies of AI bot traffic show crawlers rarely request the file.

### Is llms.txt the same as robots.txt?

No. robots.txt controls which crawlers can access your site; llms.txt only suggests which pages matter and can't block anything.

### What should I do instead to appear in AI answers?

Allow AI crawlers, add structured data, write answer-first pages with clear prices, and earn reviews and mentions on trusted UK sites.

# Outsourced Marketing Team vs Agency vs In-House: UK Costs Compared (2026)

Quick answer: A single in-house marketing hire in the UK costs 35–45% more than their salary once you add National Insurance, pension, recruitment, tools and training: a £30,000 content manager really costs about £51,000 a year (£4,300 a month). Specialist agencies typically charge £2,000–£10,000 a month, and a three-person in-house team outside London costs £130,000–£180,000 a year. For small businesses, productised outsourced teams cost far less: ContentFellow's Growth Fellow is £389 a month for five specialists. (Updated October 2026.)

## UK marketing costs at a glance

Sources: MarketingMary's UK analysis (2026) gives the 35–45% hidden-cost figure, the £51,000 loaded cost of a £30,000 content manager, the £130,000–£180,000 three-person team cost outside London, and agency ranges of £2,000–£5,000 a month for boutique SEO, £5,000–£10,000 for content agencies and £12,000–£25,000 for full-service B2B agencies.

## The hidden costs of hiring in-house

The salary is only the start. On top of it you pay:

- Employer costs: National Insurance, auto-enrolment pension, holiday and sick cover.

- Hiring costs: recruitment fees of £4,000–£5,000 per hire, and a three-to-six month ramp-up before they're fully productive. If they leave, you pay it again.

- Tools: design, video, scheduling and SEO software, plus a laptop and phone. Often £1,500–£2,000 a year.

- The skills gap: one person is rarely great at video, social, web, SEO and analytics at once. You get one strength and four compromises.

That doesn't make in-house wrong. It makes it right at scale: MarketingMary's analysis finds in-house teams become more cost-efficient once annual marketing spend passes roughly £120,000–£150,000.

## Agency vs outsourced team: what's the difference?

- A traditional agency usually sells strategy and campaigns on a retainer, often with a 6 to 12 month contract, account managers and monthly meetings. Great for bigger budgets; heavy for a 5-person business.

- An outsourced marketing team gives you the people who do the work (shooting, editing, posting, building, optimising) on a simpler monthly arrangement, often productised with fixed deliverables.

- Freelancers give you specialists, but you become the project manager, which costs your time.

## Which option fits your business?

Your situation | 
Sensible choice | 

Under £1,000 a month to spend | 
A productised team or one or two freelancers | 

One channel clearly drives sales (e.g. Google) | 
A specialist for that channel, plus basics elsewhere | 

£2,000–£10,000 a month, growing fast | 
An agency or a hybrid: one internal owner plus outside specialists | 

£150,000+ a year and daily marketing work | 
Start building in-house, keep specialists for gaps | 

Whatever you choose, one strategy across channels matters more than the model. Five freelancers each doing their own thing rarely add up to a plan.

## What can you get for under £400 a month?

At small-business budgets, the most useful mix is usually:

- Regular content: a monthly shoot and short videos (video production costs, video editing costs)

- Consistent social posting (social media management costs)

- A website that converts and stays updated (website costs)

- SEO and GEO so Google and AI assistants recommend you (GEO vs SEO)

- One monthly report that ties it together

Bought separately from freelancers, that list can easily pass £2,000 a month.

## Questions to ask any marketing provider

- Who exactly does the work, and who is my main contact?

- What are the monthly deliverables, in numbers?

- What's the minimum term and notice period?

- Do I own the content, accounts, website and data?

- How do you report results, and how often?

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does it cost to hire a marketing manager in the UK?

Expect the real cost to be 35–45% above the salary. A £30,000 content manager costs about £51,000 a year once National Insurance, pension, recruitment, tools and training are included.

### Is outsourcing marketing cheaper than hiring in-house?

For most small businesses, yes. In-house teams tend to become more cost-efficient only once marketing spend passes roughly £120,000–£150,000 a year.

### How much does a marketing agency cost per month in the UK?

Specialist agencies typically charge £2,000–£5,000 a month for one channel, content agencies £5,000–£10,000, and full-service agencies £12,000–£25,000 or more.

### What is a productised marketing service?

A service sold like a product: fixed deliverables at a fixed monthly price, rather than hours or open-ended retainers. It suits small businesses that want predictable costs.

### What is a hybrid marketing model?

One person inside the business owns marketing and decisions, while outside specialists do the execution. Many growing UK SMEs use it.

# How Much Does a Small Business Website Cost in the UK in 2026?

Quick answer: A UK small business website costs anywhere from £200 to £20,000 to build, plus £5 to £150 a month to keep running. A DIY site on Wix or Squarespace costs roughly £9–£40 a month, a freelancer typically charges £500–£2,500, and most agencies quote £3,000–£10,000 for a properly built small business site. Monthly website plans spread the cost instead: ContentFellow's Build Fellow is £69 a month including hosting and updates. (Updated October 2026.)

Sources: Authentic Style puts UK websites at £200–£20,000, with most small businesses budgeting £3,000–£10,000. Hollis Web quotes £500–£2,500 for a basic UK site and £2,000–£8,000 for ecommerce. GoDaddy says most small businesses are fine on hosting at £3.99–£16.99 a month.

## The real cost is build plus run

The design quote is only part of the bill. Budget for all four:

- Design and build: layout, pages, mobile version, speed, copy and images.

- Domain and hosting: about £10–£15 a year for a .co.uk or .com domain, and £4–£17 a month for decent small business hosting with an SSL certificate.

- Care and updates: security patches, backups, plugin updates and small text changes. Agencies typically charge from £50 a month for this.

- Growth: new pages, a booking system, a shop, and the SEO and GEO work that gets you found.

## What makes a website cost more?

- Number of pages. A five-page site (home, services, about, reviews, contact) is a very different job from 30 pages.

- Custom design vs template. Templates are cheaper; a custom design fits your brand and is easier to stand out with.

- Copywriting. If you write the words, it's cheaper. Good copy is often what makes a site actually win enquiries.

- Features. Booking, payments, a shop, member areas and integrations with your CRM all add cost.

- SEO and GEO set-up. Structured data, page speed, and service pages built for Google and AI search. Read our guide on how to get your business recommended by ChatGPT to see why this matters in 2026.

## DIY, freelancer, agency or monthly plan?

- DIY suits you if you have time, a simple offer and a good eye. The cost is your hours: a basic site often takes 30 to 60 of them.

- A freelancer can be great value. Check their recent work, who hosts the site, and what happens if they're unavailable.

- An agency makes sense for complex sites, ecommerce at scale, or when you need a team to own the project.

- A monthly plan suits small businesses that want a custom site, hosting, security and regular changes for one predictable fee.

## Questions to ask any website provider

- Who owns the domain, the design and the content?

- Where is it hosted, and who handles security and backups?

- How many changes a month are included, and what do extras cost?

- Will the site have structured data, fast mobile pages and a sitemap?

- Is there a minimum term? What happens to the site if I leave?

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does a basic website cost in the UK?

A basic five-page UK small business website typically costs £500 to £2,500 from a freelancer or £3,000 or more from an agency, plus £5 to £150 a month for hosting and care.

### How much does a website cost per month in the UK?

Running costs are usually £5 to £150 a month: hosting from about £4, a website builder plan from £9, and a maintenance plan from about £50. Monthly website plans like the Build Fellow cost £69 including everything.

### Is Wix or Squarespace cheaper than a web designer?

Upfront, yes: plans cost roughly £9 to £40 a month. But you do the work, and a basic site typically takes 30 to 60 hours to build well.

### How long does it take to build a small business website?

A simple five-page site usually takes two to six weeks, depending mostly on how quickly copy, photos and feedback are ready.

### Do I need to pay for website maintenance?

Someone has to update software, keep backups and fix security issues. You can do it yourself, but an unmaintained site is a common way small businesses get hacked or go offline.

### Does a new website help with Google and ChatGPT?

Only if it's built for search: fast pages, clear service pages with prices and locations, structured data and a sitemap. Ask for these in writing.

# How Much Does Social Media Management Cost in the UK? (2026 Prices)

Quick answer: Most UK small businesses pay £300 to £1,500 a month for professional social media management, not counting ad spend. A freelancer typically charges £300–£1,000 a month, an agency £1,250–£3,500 per channel, and a full-time in-house social media manager costs about £3,290 a month once employer costs are added. Productised monthly plans start lower: ContentFellow's Social Fellow is from £59 a month. (Updated October 2026.)

## What does social media management actually include?

"Social media management" means different things to different people, which is why quotes vary so much. A full service usually covers:

- Strategy: which platforms, what to post, who you're talking to

- Content: writing captions, designing graphics, editing short videos

- Scheduling and posting: getting it out at the right times

- Community management: replying to comments and messages

- Trend research: spotting sounds, formats and topics before they peak

- Reporting: what worked, what didn't, what's next

Cheaper quotes often cover only scheduling and posting. Before comparing prices, ask exactly which of these six jobs is included.

## UK social media management prices in 2026

Option | 
Typical monthly cost | 
What you usually get | 
Best for | 

Do it yourself | 
£0–£50 (tools) | 
Your own time, a scheduler like Buffer or Meta Business Suite | 
Very early businesses with spare hours | 

Freelancer | 
£300–£1,000 | 
1–3 platforms, posting and some content |

Sources: Birdeye's UK pricing guide puts most UK social media marketing at £500–£5,000 a month. Kraken's 2026 analysis puts single-channel agency retainers at £1,250–£3,500 (Whito data) and the average UK freelance social media day rate at £334 (YunoJuno).

## Why is an in-house social media manager so expensive?

The average UK social media manager salary is £34,229 (Indeed, June 2026). Add employer National Insurance and pension and the real cost is around £39,500 a year, or £3,290 a month, before recruitment, software and training. You also get one person's skills: someone great at TikTok may be weaker at LinkedIn or design.

For most businesses with under 20 staff, that's more than social media will return. An outside service gives you a team's skills for a fraction of the cost.

## What drives the price up or down?

- Number of platforms. Each extra channel adds planning, formatting and community time. Three platforms done well beats six done badly.

- Posting volume. Three posts a week is a different job from daily posting with Stories and Reels.

- Who creates the content. If you supply photos and videos, management is cheaper. If the manager has to shoot or edit video, the price jumps. That's why many businesses pair management with a separate video editing or video production service.

- Paid ads. Ad spend goes to Meta or TikTok, not the manager. Managers usually charge a separate fee to run ads, either flat or 10–20% of spend.

## How much should a UK small business budget?

- Sole trader or new business: £0–£150 a month. Post yourself with a scheduler, or use a low-cost managed plan so it actually happens every week.

- Local service business (cafés, salons, trades, clinics): £150–£500 a month. Customers check your feed before they book, so it needs to look active and current.

- Growing business with a sales team or online shop: £500–£1,500 a month, often with a small ad budget on top.

Keep social media in proportion. It builds trust and keeps you front of mind, but for many local businesses Google and AI search bring more new customers. Our guide to GEO vs SEO explains how those work.

## Questions to ask before you sign

- Which platforms, and how many posts, Stories and Reels per week?

- Who creates the images and videos, and how many rounds of changes do I get?

- Do you reply to comments and messages? Within what time?

- Do I own the accounts and all the content if we stop?

- Is there a minimum contract, and what's the notice period?

- What does the monthly report show?

A good provider answers all six in writing.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does social media management cost per month in the UK?

Most UK small businesses pay £300 to £1,500 a month, excluding ad spend. Freelancers charge £300–£1,000, agencies £1,250–£3,500 per channel, and monthly plans like the Social Fellow start from £59.

### Is £300 a month enough for social media management?

Yes, for one to three platforms with regular posting and content you partly supply. It usually won't cover heavy video production, paid ads management or daily community replies.

### How much does a freelance social media manager charge in the UK?

The average UK freelance social media day rate is about £334, or around £42 an hour. Monthly retainers for small businesses usually fall between £300 and £1,000.

### Does social media management include paid ads?

Not usually. Ad spend is paid to the platform, and managing ads is often a separate fee. Always ask whether ads are included before comparing quotes.

### How many platforms should a small business be on?

Two or three, chosen by where your customers spend time. Facebook and Instagram suit most local businesses, LinkedIn suits B2B, and TikTok suits younger audiences.

### Can I cancel a social media management contract?

It depends on the provider. Many agencies ask for 3 to 12 months. ContentFellow bills monthly and you can change or remove your Fellow from the next month.

# How Much Does Video Editing Cost in the UK? Reels, YouTube and Podcasts (2026)

Quick answer: UK freelance video editors typically charge £25 to £75 an hour, £50 to £400 a day, or £50 to £200 per finished minute. A short Reel or TikTok usually costs £30–£150 to edit, a 10-minute YouTube video £150–£600, and a one-hour podcast £75–£300. If you need videos every week, a monthly plan is often cheaper: ContentFellow's Creator Fellow is £119 a month for 8 short videos, a motion graphics video and a podcast edit. (Updated October 2026.)

## UK video editing rates in 2026

Pricing model | 
Typical UK rate | 
When it's used | 

Per hour | 
£25–£75 | 
Small or unpredictable jobs | 

Per day | 
£50–£400 | 
Larger projects, agency freelancers |

Sources: Wise's UK guide puts freelance video editors at £50 to around £400 a day. John Isaacson's UK pricing guide lists £25–£75 an hour, £50–£200 per finished minute and £100–£2,000+ per project.

## Prices by format

Format | 
Typical UK freelance price | 
What affects it | 

Short Reel / TikTok / Short (15–60s) | 
£30–£150 each | 
Captions, B-roll, hooks, trend edits | 

YouTube video (8–15 min) | 
£150–£600 each |

£300–£1,500 | 
Interviews, colour grading, music licences | 

These ranges are drawn from the hourly and per-minute rates above. Beginners charge less and specialist motion designers charge more.

## What makes an edit cost more?

- Raw footage. An editor has to watch everything you send. Three hours of footage for a 60-second Reel takes longer than 10 minutes of footage.

- Style. Simple cuts are quick. Animated captions, B-roll, sound design and motion graphics add hours.

- Format. Vertical short-form needs strong hooks and fast pacing; long-form needs structure; podcasts need multi-camera switching and audio clean-up.

- Turnaround and revisions. Rush jobs cost extra, and every extra round of changes is more time.

The cheapest way to cut editing costs is better footage: good sound, steady shots and less of it. If you're not filming yet, see our guide to video production costs in the UK.

## Freelancer, agency or monthly plan?

- Freelancer: best for one-off projects, or if you find a reliable editor who understands your brand. Watch for availability, briefing time and inconsistent turnaround.

- Agency: best for ads and polished campaigns, with higher prices to match.

- Monthly plan: best when you need a steady flow (weekly Reels, a monthly podcast) at a fixed price.

### The monthly maths

Eight Reels a month at a typical £50 freelance rate is £400, before a podcast edit or any motion graphics. A monthly plan that covers all three at a flat fee is usually cheaper and saves you rebriefing someone each time.

## Questions to ask a video editor

- How many revision rounds are included?

- What's the turnaround for each format?

- Will you add captions, and are they burned in or separate files?

- Is music licensed for commercial use on social media?

- Do I get the project files, or only the finished videos?

- Can you work from my brand fonts, colours and templates?

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does a video editor cost per hour in the UK?

UK freelance video editors typically charge £25 to £75 an hour. Beginners sit at the lower end, while experienced editors and motion designers charge more.

### How much does it cost to edit a Reel or TikTok?

Usually £30 to £150 per video from a UK freelancer, depending on captions, B-roll and how much raw footage there is. Monthly plans bring the per-video price down.

### How much does podcast editing cost in the UK?

A one-hour podcast typically costs £75 to £300 to edit, more if it's filmed with several cameras or needs short clips cut for social media.

### How long does it take to edit a video?

A simple Reel can take one to two hours; a 10-minute YouTube video often takes a full day. Turnaround depends on the editor's workload and revision rounds.

### Is it cheaper to edit videos myself?

Apps like CapCut make basic edits easy and free. The cost is time: most business owners find a few hours a week of editing isn't the best use of it.

### Should I pay per video or monthly?

Pay per video for occasional one-offs. If you post every week, a monthly plan usually costs less and gives you consistent quality and turnaround.

# How Much Does Video Production Cost for UK Small Businesses? (2026)

Quick answer: A UK freelance videographer typically charges £200 to £900 a day, depending on experience and location, plus editing. A London crew day can cost £1,500–£2,500, and production companies usually quote £2,000 or more per project. For regular content rather than one big film, monthly shoots are often better value: ContentFellow's Studio Fellow is £149 a month for one on-site shoot with photo and 4K video. (Updated October 2026.)

## UK video production prices in 2026

Option | 
Typical cost | 
What you usually get | 
Best for | 

Phone + DIY | 
£0–£300 (kit) | 
Your own footage, your own time | 
Quick behind-the-scenes clips | 

Freelance videographer | 
£200–£900 a day | 
One person shooting; editing often extra | 
One-off promos, events, testimonials | 

London crew day | 
£1,500–£2,500 | 
Camera operator, sound, lighting | 
Polished brand films | 

Production company | 
£2,000–£20,000+ per project | 
Script, crew, edit, music, revisions | 
Adverts and flagship brand films | 

Monthly shoots (Studio Fellow) | 
£149 a month | 
One on-site shoot up to 3 hours, photo + 4K video | 
Steady content for social, website and ads | 

Sources: Creative Clan puts a solo London videographer at £400–£900 a day. UK videographers on Reddit and Facebook groups report day rates from £200 outside London to £450 plus expenses as a common mid-level rate, and £1,500–£2,500 for London client shoot days.

## Where your video budget goes

Every video quote, from a freelancer or a production company, is made of four parts. Ask for each as a separate line:

- Pre-production: the brief, script or outline, shot list, locations, and who appears on camera.

- Shoot day: crew size, hours, camera and lighting kit, travel and expenses.

- Post-production: editing, colour grading, sound, music licences and captions.

- Delivery: formats (16:9 for YouTube and your website, 9:16 for Reels and TikTok), cut-downs for social, and rounds of revisions.

The biggest hidden cost is usually post-production. A day of shooting can easily need two days of editing. If a quote seems cheap, check whether editing is included at all. Our guide to video editing costs in the UK has the numbers.

## What makes a shoot cost more?

- Crew size. A solo shooter is cheapest. Adding sound, lighting and a director multiplies the day rate.

- Location. London rates run higher, and travel and parking add up.

- Scripted vs documentary. Scripted adverts with actors need far more planning than filming your team at work.

- Licensing. Commercial music, stock footage and actors' usage rights can cost more than the shoot.

- Volume of outputs. One three-minute film is a different job from twenty short clips for social media.

## What does a small business actually need?

Most small businesses don't need a cinematic brand film. They need a steady supply of good, honest content:

- Short clips of you and your team at work

- Customer testimonials

- Product or service close-ups

- Professional photos for the website, Google Business Profile and social

That's why regular short shoots usually beat one expensive production day. Fresh content each month keeps your social feeds active, gives AI search engines and Google something current to find, and costs less over a year.

## Example yearly budgets

Approach | 
Example | 
Rough yearly cost | 

One freelance day a quarter | 
4 × (£450 shoot + £450 edit) | 
~£3,600 | 

One production company film | 
1 brand film | 
£2,000–£10,000 |

£1,788 | 

## Questions to ask before you book

- Is editing included, and how many finished videos and photos do I get?

- Which formats are delivered (landscape, vertical, square)?

- How many rounds of revisions are included?

- Is music licensed for commercial and social use?

- Who owns the footage, and can I use it in paid ads?

- Are travel and expenses included?

UK freelance videographers usually charge £200 to £900 a day. Mid-level rates of around £450 plus expenses are common outside London, and London crew days often cost £1,500 or more.

# Website Subscription vs One-Off Build: Which Is Cheaper for UK Small Businesses?

Quick answer: Over three years, a one-off website plus a basic care plan usually costs £2,100 to £3,300 with a small provider, while a website subscription costs about £2,500 at £69 a month and includes changes. Buy outright if you have the cash and rarely change your site. Choose a subscription if you want no upfront bill and regular updates. Agency builds at £3,000–£10,000 cost more either way. (UK prices, October 2026.)

## What's the difference?

- One-off build: you pay once for the design and build, then you own the site. Hosting, security and changes are extra, either paid as you go or on a care plan.

- Website subscription (pay monthly): you pay a fixed monthly fee that covers the build, hosting, security and a set number of changes. There's little or no upfront cost.

## Three-year cost, side by side

Option | 
Upfront | 
Monthly | 
Total over 3 years | 

Budget one-off (e.g. £499) + basic care £29.99/mo |

about £1,580 |

£50 |

£4,500 | 
£100 | 
about £8,100 | 

UK reference prices: Juggernaut Tech sells one-off sites from £499 plus £29.99 a month, freelancers typically charge £500–£3,000, and GoDaddy's UK guide puts a basic agency design at about £4,500.

## When is a one-off build better?

- You have £349 to £1,499 available now and want to own the site outright.

- Your site rarely changes: a brochure site you update a few times a year.

- You (or someone on your team) can handle small edits yourself.

Even then, budget for hosting, security and backups. A site with no care plan is the one that gets hacked or breaks after an update.

## When is a subscription better?

- You don't want a big upfront bill.

- You change prices, offers or photos most months.

- You'd rather have one supplier responsible for everything.

Watch for minimum terms and exit fees. A fair subscription tells you up front what happens if you leave and whether you can take the site with you.

- Monthly plans: Care £49, Build Fellow £69 (site included), Care Plus £159 (see management plans).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a website subscription worth it?

It's worth it if you want no upfront cost and regular changes. Over three years it often costs about the same as a one-off build plus a care plan, but with changes included.

### Do I own my website on a subscription?

It depends on the contract. Check whether you can take your site and domain with you if you leave, and what that costs.

### How much does a one-off website cost in the UK?

Small business websites typically cost £400 to £3,000 from budget providers and freelancers, and £3,000 to £10,000 from agencies.

### Do I still need to pay monthly after a one-off build?

Usually yes, for hosting, security and backups. Basic care plans start at around £30 to £50 a month.

### Which is better for SEO?

Neither on its own. What matters is fast pages, clear service pages, structured data and regular updates, which are easier when someone looks after the site every month.
